html:
African grain crops, above all pearl millet and sorghum, that reached western India around 2000 BCE and became staples of dry farming there.

Both were first grown in Africa: pearl millet in the Sahel of West Africa and sorghum in the savanna to the east. How they crossed the Arabian Sea is not certain. Most likely they moved along the coastal trade that linked Africa, Arabia and the late Indus Valley civilisation. Finger millet and some pulses made the same trip.

These crops mattered because they need little rain. In Gujarat, Rajasthan and the Deccan, where wheat and rice struggle, millet and sorghum fed villages through the hot season. They still do: India grows more pearl millet than any other country, where it is called bajra, and sorghum is jowar. The exchange ran both ways, as Asian crops went to Africa in turn.
sum: African grain crops, above all pearl millet and sorghum, that reached western India around 2000 BCE and became staples of dry farming there.
